#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA annual return officer particulars** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** From 20 October 2026, an annual-return filer must confirm that current particulars already provided to ACRA are accurate for directors, chief executive officers (CEOs), secretaries, auditors and relevant members. These particulars include names, identification details, nationality, contact address, appointment dates, registered office address and shareholding details where applicable. The form separately asks whether any individual performs the CEO role. A company limited by guarantee must confirm its latest-reported total member count. Applies to annual returns filed from the expressly stated commencement date. Check ACRA-recorded particulars and update inaccurate particulars in Bizfile before filing. The CEO question concerns individuals performing the role; the ACRA notice does not limit it to a title or appointed position. Companies limited by guarantee have an additional total-number-of-members confirmation. The notice does not say the CEO question or officer-particulars confirmation changes the underlying duty to appoint or register officers. A case-specific conclusion requires: For a particular filing: filing date, company type, existing ACRA particulars, whether individuals perform the CEO role, and whether the company is limited by guarantee. General change explanation only; does not verify what particulars are currently recorded for an entity. Do not apply this change to filings submitted before 20 October 2026 without contemporaneous evidence. The notice gives examples of particulars and says “where applicable”; it is not a field-by-field eform schema. rows.before:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA financial statement preparation and filing exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says all Singapore-incorporated companies must prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies, and must file them unless exempted. A solvent exempt private company may qualify not to file; dormant-relevant-company relief requires all Companies Act section 201A conditions. Newly incorporated or inactive status alone is not listed as an exemption in this guidance. For required filings, ACRA lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL without a separate PDF copy for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. The Full/Simplified/FSH/PDF template depends on the company’s exact status and regulatory category. Dormant relevant companies need not prepare/file only if all Companies Act section 201A requirements are met, including the assets, dormancy and listing/subsidiary conditions. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. A case-specific conclusion requires: Local/foreign incorporation, company form and whether it is a company limited by guarantee. Required-to-file/exempt status, dormancy history, listed/subsidiary status and group assets. Current-year revenue and assets, consolidation and currency facts. Public-accountability or MAS regulatory status. EPC status and solvency, where relevant. Does not determine an individual company’s template without classification facts. The complete definitions and section 201A eligibility must be checked against ACRA’s linked guidance and law. Do not apply the current page or 19 October 2026 XBRL boundary to a historical filing unless the relevant year-specific official source supports it. **ACRA financial statement preparation and filing exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says all Singapore-incorporated companies must prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies, and must file them unless exempted. Newly incorporated or inactive status alone is not listed as an exemption in this guidance. For required filings, ACRA lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL without a separate PDF copy for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. #### IRAS — GST

**GST input tax on staff medical expenses** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS states that staff medical input tax is generally disallowed under regulation 26 of the GST (General) Regulations. Subject to the ordinary input-tax conditions, the stated exceptions are expenses obligatory under WICA or a qualifying Industrial Relations Act collective agreement; or, for expenses incurred on or after 1 October 2021, treatment connected with a work-related health risk or requirement and required under relevant Singapore written law. For the advisory limb, IRAS specifies treatment related to COVID-19 and required under a written advisory of the Government or a Singapore public authority. IRAS specifically says Primary Care Plan expenses do not meet the described work-related exception. A claim needs the expense date, legal/collective-agreement basis, work-related risk and mandate evidence, GST registration and invoice facts. [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on staff medical expenses): No, GST incurred on PCP will not be claimable. rows.question: Can a business recover GST on a chauffeured point-to-point private-hire ride instead of buying or hiring the motor car itself?
rows.before:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

#### IRAS — GST

**Status:** Evidence verified

**GST input tax on business motor cars** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally disallows input tax on a motor car’s purchase and running costs under regulation 27, unless the vehicle is outside the regulation 25(1) motor-car definition or a specific exception applies. Its examples include qualifying chauffeured pay-per-trip transport services from 1 April 2022; qualifying costs for cars used by a third party from 1 January 2023; and vehicles such as lorries, vans and motorcycles that are not motor cars. Costs for cars used physically or economically by you or your employees remain disallowed. For a connected person’s car, the claimant must recover the expense and the recovery must not be ancillary to a primary supply; partial recovery limits the claim to the recovered portion. If only half the expenses are recovered, the exception permits input tax only to the extent of that half, not the unrecovered half. All exceptions remain subject to the ordinary claim conditions and records. [IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/goods-services-tax-(gst)/claiming-gst-(input-tax)/conditions-for-claiming-input-tax)

**Source:** IRAS | Conditions for Claiming Input Tax (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on business motor cars): Input tax claims on purchase and running expenses of motor cars are disallowed under Regulation 27 of the GST (General) Regulations unless the car is excluded from the definition of a 'motor car' in Regulation 25(1). In addition, input tax incurred for specific scenarios is also excluded from the scope of Regulation 27. The input tax incurred in such specific scenarios will be claimable, subject to the conditions for input tax claim.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on business motor cars): Yes, from 1 Apr 2022 onwards, you can claim input tax incurred on the purchase of services to transport passengers from point A to point B (pay-per-trip) in a chauffeured private hire car (e.g. airport transfer services), if the conditions for claiming input tax are met. This includes ensuring that your purchases are supported by valid tax invoices or simplified tax invoices with GST charged to you. For example, for limousine services, you will need to keep an invoice from the GST-registered business showing that GST has been charged on the services.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports GST input tax on business motor cars): Yes, from 1 Jan 2023, where you incur expenses on a motor car that is used by a third party, you will be allowed input tax claims on the cost and running expenses of the motor car incurred, if the conditions for claiming input tax are met

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Withholding tax filing and payment deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS requires WHT filing and payment by the 15th of the second month after its defined date of payment. For most payments, use the earliest of the contractual due date (or invoice date if there is no agreement, ignoring credit terms), credit to an account designated by the non-resident, and actual payment. Director fees have separate timing rules based on arrears/advance approval, entitlement, credit and actual payment. WHT still must be filed when a DTA or ARI makes the rate zero. GIRO is normally deducted on the 25th of the due month, or the next working day if that date is a weekend/public holiday. The exact deadline requires the payment type and all relevant dates. [IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/withholding-tax-filing/withholding-tax-filing-and-payment-due-date)

**Source:** IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

Determine your employees’ CPF contributions

Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status

Determine the year of SPR status

The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion

As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Final salary payment deadlines by termination reason** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** For employees covered by the Employment Act, final salary is due on the last employment day when required notice is served; within 7 days of the last employment day when the employee resigns without notice; and, after misconduct dismissal or employer termination, on the last day or, if that is not possible, within 3 working days from dismissal or termination. Commission timing follows the employment contract or existing policies or practices. For a foreign employee leaving employment, the employer must withhold monies due for tax clearance for up to 30 days after notifying the Comptroller of Income Tax; this can affect when salary is released. [MOM | Paying salary](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/salary/paying-salary)

**Source:** MOM | Paying salary (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Final salary payment deadlines by termination reason): If you are covered by the Employment Act, your employer must pay your salary at least once a month.
They can also pay it at shorter intervals if they choose.
Salary must be paid:
Within 7 days after the end of the salary period.
For overtime work, within 14 days after the end of the salary period.

Your final salary payment could vary depending on the following situations:
In this situation | Your final salary must be paid
Employee resigns and serves the required notice period | On the last day of employment.
Employee resigns and does not serve the notice period | Within 7 days of the last day of employment.
Dismissal on grounds of misconduct | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of dismissal.
Employer terminates the contract | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of termination.

If your contract involves commission, how and when the commission is paid depends on what is in your employment contract or existing policies or practices.
If you’re a foreign employee who is leaving your employment, your employer is required to withhold all your monies due to you for tax clearance for up to 30 days upon giving notice of the cessation of your employment to the Comptroller of Income Tax. The monies include your salary, leave pay, etc.
- Official source: [MOM | Paying salary](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/salary/paying-salary)

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Public holiday entitlement and pay** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee has 11 paid public holidays each year. If a holiday falls on the rest day, the following working day will be a paid public holiday; if it falls on a non-working day, another day off or an extra day at the gross rate is due. Working on a public holiday ordinarily earns holiday gross pay plus an additional day at the basic rate; overtime applies beyond normal hours. By mutual agreement, the day may be substituted. Part IV coverage limits which employees may use time off in lieu. Distinguish a holiday on a working day, non-working day, or rest day. For holiday gross pay, the employee must not be absent without consent or reasonable excuse on the working day immediately before or after the holiday; authorised leave on either day is permitted. No holiday pay is due when the holiday itself falls during approved unpaid leave. Additional basic-rate pay is the default for working on the holiday; substitute-holiday arrangements require mutual agreement. An employee outside Employment Act coverage is governed by the contract. Time off in lieu of hours worked is available only to employees not covered by Part IV under the stated arrangement. Rest-day pay and any excess-hours overtime are separate entitlements. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act and Part IV coverage. Work schedule and whether the date is a working, non-working or rest day. Whether the employee worked, hours worked, agreed substitution/time-off arrangements, and relevant absence or unpaid-leave facts. Does not decide a specific date’s gazetted holiday status or compute holiday pay without schedule and wage facts. Does not replace separate rest-day, overtime or part-time rules. [MOM | Public holidays: entitlement and pay](https://www.mom.gov.sg/employment-practices/public-holidays-entitlement-and-pay)

#### Monetary Authority of Singapore — Financial regulation

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MAS LFMC financial returns and SFA reporting requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS’s 29 May 2026 SFA compliance toolkit states that an LFMC files quarterly Forms 1 and 2 within 14 days after each quarter end under Regulation 27 of the FMR. It also lists annual audited Forms 1 to 6 and the audited Profit and Loss Account, Balance Sheet and auditor’s report (including a management letter, if any) within five months after financial year end under section 107 of the SFA and Regulation 27 of the FMR. The toolkit says it is non-exhaustive and excludes obligations outside the SFA and fund-level requirements. Confirm the entity’s LFMC scope, reporting period, and current MAS-Tx instructions before applying these deadlines. A complete reporting calendar also needs the licence and manager regime, regulated activities, fund types and reporting periods, plus checks for event-triggered notifications and duties outside this toolkit. One quarterly financial return does not establish that all MAS duties are discharged. [LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES](https://www.mas.gov.sg/-/media/mas-media-library/regulation/guidance/cmi/compliance-toolkits-for-fund-management-companies/sfa-compliance-toolkit-lfmcs29-may-2026-clean.pdf)

**Source:** LICENSED FUND MANAGEMENT COMPANIES (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports MAS LFMC financial returns and SFA reporting requirements): This compliance toolkit aims to provide LFMCs with a simple reference on the common applications, forms and submissions pursuant to the SFA that are applicable to LFMCs. However, it is not exhaustive, and LFMCs are expected to be familiar with all legislations and requirements that are applicable to them. For the avoidance of doubt, this toolkit excludes reporting obligations that fall outside the SFA; as well as fund-level requirements (e.g. Code of Collective Investment Scheme). Where an LFMC intends to apply for or holds a CMS licence to carry on business in other SFA regulated activities such as dealing in Capital Markets Products, it should also refer to the compliance toolkit that is relevant to these other types of regulated activities. **SFA 04-N24 reporting of misconduct by representatives from 1 January 2027** (party in scope: Company)
- **MAS rule explanation:** MAS Notice SFA 04-N24 takes effect on 1 January 2027. It applies to CMS licence holders and persons exempt under SFA section 99(1)(a)–(d), for misconduct by their representatives and former representatives. A CMI must submit a Misconduct Report no later than 21 calendar days after the date it first has reasonable grounds to believe the current or former representative committed misconduct during the representative period, unless the Authority allows a longer period in writing. Paragraph 21 keeps the cancelled Notice applicable where a report was submitted before 1 January 2027 or was required by 31 December 2026. Paragraph 20 addresses a pre-2027 reasonable-grounds case where no Misconduct Report in the form set out in the cancelled Notice had been submitted by 1 January 2027: the report under SFA 04-N24 is due within 21 calendar days after 1 January 2027, or a longer period allowed in writing. A case-specific conclusion requires the CMI status, representative period, reasonable-grounds date and transition facts. The ordinary SFA 04-N24 rule is not yet in effect for an October or December 2026 matter. The 2027 notice does not by itself establish what earlier reporting duty applied or prove that none existed. Paragraph 21 must be checked first: it continues the cancelled Notice for matters with a report already submitted before 1 January 2027 or due by 31 December 2026. rows.question: Our company needs to file financial statements. For Simplified XBRL, is being non-publicly accountable enough, or do both revenue and total assets also have to be at most S$500,000?
rows.before:
### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**General statutory guidance:** Verified for all listed issues.
**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says all Singapore-incorporated companies must prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies, and must file them unless exempted. A solvent exempt private company may qualify not to file; dormant-relevant-company relief requires all Companies Act section 201A conditions. Newly incorporated or inactive status alone is not listed as an exemption in this guidance. For required filings, ACRA lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL without a separate PDF copy for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. The Full/Simplified/FSH/PDF template depends on the company’s exact status and regulatory category. Dormant relevant companies need not prepare/file only if all Companies Act section 201A requirements are met, including the assets, dormancy and listing/subsidiary conditions. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. A case-specific conclusion requires: Local/foreign incorporation, company form and whether it is a company limited by guarantee. Required-to-file/exempt status, dormancy history, listed/subsidiary status and group assets. Current-year revenue and assets, consolidation and currency facts. Public-accountability or MAS regulatory status. EPC status and solvency, where relevant. Does not determine an individual company’s template without classification facts. The complete definitions and section 201A eligibility must be checked against ACRA’s linked guidance and law. Do not apply the current page or 19 October 2026 XBRL boundary to a historical filing unless the relevant year-specific official source supports it. **ECI filing and waiver requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. #### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Withholding tax on non-resident service payments** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS says WHT applies to specified service and management fees paid to a non-resident company to the extent attributable to work done in Singapore; a mixed Singapore/overseas engagement must be apportioned. Services supplied electronically from overseas without sending staff are described as performed outside Singapore. The current page states the prevailing 17% Corporate Income Tax rate on gross service fees for Singapore work, but the applicable DTA, payee residence and permanent-establishment facts may change the rate or treatment. IRAS also says the old related-party cost-pooling concession was withdrawn for payments liable on or after 1 November 2022. Specific treatment requires the payee type and residence, service scope/location, DTA and relevant dates. [IRAS | Payments that are subject to withholding tax](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/payments-to-non-resident-company/payments-that-are-subject-to-withholding-tax)

**Source:** IRAS | Payments that are subject to withholding tax (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax on non-resident service payments): Where payment is made to a non-resident company for the installation of equipment, technical support services, training, consultancy or other services provided by the non-resident company in connection with the application or use of scientific, technical, industrial or commercial knowledge or information, withholding tax is applicable on the service fees attributable to the work done in Singapore.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax on non-resident service payments): Similarly, where payment is made to a non-resident company for the management or assistance in the management of any trade, business or profession, withholding tax is applicable on the management fees attributable to the work done in Singapore.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax on non-resident service payments): However, if the non-resident company provides the services via electronic means from overseas (e.g. internet presentation, email and telephone) without sending staff to Singapore, the services are rendered outside Singapore and withholding tax is not applicable.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax on non-resident service payments): Where cost reimbursement payment is made on or before 31 Oct 2022 to a non-resident related party for services rendered in Singapore under a cost-pooling arrangement, and the cost-pooling conditions stated in the e-Tax Guide on Transfer Pricing Guidelines (PDF, 1.6MB) have been satisfied, withholding tax is not applicable on such payment. With effect from 1 Nov 2022, this administrative concession will be withdrawn. Withholding tax will be applicable to any cost reimbursement payment liable to be made on or after 1 Nov 2022 to a non-resident related party, even if the payment is made under a cost-pooling arrangement.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax on non-resident service payments): For services performed in Singapore, withholding tax is to be imposed at the prevailing Corporate Income Tax rate of 17% on the gross service fees. This is not the final tax. If the non-resident company wishes to claim deduction for the expenses incurred in deriving the service income, it must submit the certified accounts and tax computation for IRAS' examination. When the net income and tax have been determined, any tax withheld in excess of the tax on the net income will be refunded.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax on non-resident service payments): If the company is a resident of a jurisdiction with which Singapore has an Avoidance of Double Tax Agreement (DTA), the DTA may provide for relief from double taxation, depending on the provision of the DTA.

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

#### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF additional wage ceiling and year-end recalculation** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** CPF Board sets the AW ceiling per employer, per year at S$102,000 less that employee’s Ordinary Wages subject to CPF for the year. The 2026 examples use an OW ceiling of S$8,000 per month and say the year in which an AW is due and payable controls the ceiling. At each AW payment, estimate OW for the year and account for AW already subject to CPF. In the last month of employment or December, whichever is earlier, recalculate using actual OW subject to CPF through that period; pay any CPF shortfall with the last-month or December contributions, and apply for a refund if excess CPF contributions result. To compute the current payment’s CPF-subject AW, the employer must provide actual year-to-date OW/AW and either the expected full-year OW or confirm this is final settlement. [Examples for computation of Additional Wage (AW) Ceiling](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/sfc/servlet.shepherd/document/download/069IW00000KUuZCYA1)

The AW ceiling determines the maximum amount of AW subject to CPF contributions for the year. An employee’s AW ceiling is computed on a
per employer, per year basis. The AW ceiling applies to all Singapore Citizens and Singapore Permanent Residents (SPR).
AW ceiling Calculation
The AW ceiling is computed using the following formula:
$102,000 - Total Ordinary Wages (OW) subject to CPF for the year
For the year 2026, the AW ceiling is
$102,000 – ($8,000* x 12)
* The OW ceiling is capped at $8,000 for 2026.
Note: The applicable AW ceiling depends on the due and payable date of the AW. For example, if the 2025 bonus is due and payable to the employee in 2026, then the employer should contribute
according to the 2026 AW ceiling.
Step 1: At every AW payment, e mployers should estimate the AW ceiling by using the current year’s estimated monthly OW. Employers should
either:
a) Submit a refund application online (select the option: Refund of payments made for 1 employee/platform worker) immediately if any excess
contributions on AW are detected; or
b) Pay the shortfall in contributions on AW, if any.
Step 2: In the last month of employment or end of the year in December (whichever is earlier), employers should re-calculate the AW
ceiling based on the actual OW subject to CPF paid up till the last month of employment or in December and pay any shortfall in CPF contributions
together with the employee's contributions for his last month of employment or in December. If there are any excess CPF contributions, you
should submit a refund application online.
For the examples below, we assume that the monthly contribution rates applicable for the employee is for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third
year and onwards). If your employee is a SPR in the first or second year of SPR status, please use the applicable monthly contribution rates.

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MOM annual leave eligibility, entitlement and proration** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee becomes entitled to paid annual leave after at least 3 months; being on probation does not remove that entitlement. For 3 to 12 months of service, the entitlement is based on completed months worked even if the employee is still on probation. The minimum annual entitlement rises by one day per year from 7 days in year one to 14 days from year eight. The official formula is completed months of service divided by 12, multiplied by the annual leave entitlement; fractions less than one-half of a day round down, while half or more rounds up to one day. Approved unpaid leave is excluded; service during a resignation notice period counts. The Employment Act must cover the employee and at least three months’ service must be completed; probation does not remove entitlement after this threshold. For 3 to 12 months of service, pro-rating uses completed months even if the employee is still on probation; a partial, incomplete service month is disregarded. The minimum table follows year of service beginning on the employment start date. For employees outside the Employment Act, use contractual terms; this page does not establish their statutory entitlement. Annual leave on half-working days, unused-leave carry-forward/forfeiture and termination encashment have separate rules. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act coverage and start date. Completed service months and service year. Annual contractual entitlement, approved unpaid-leave periods, and notice period if pro-rating. States the general statutory minimum and pro-rating method; it does not calculate an individual balance without the listed facts. The current page’s retrieval or update date is not treated as legal commencement. #### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Public holiday entitlement and pay** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** An Employment Act-covered employee has 11 paid public holidays each year. If a holiday falls on the rest day, the following working day will be a paid public holiday; if it falls on a non-working day, another day off or an extra day at the gross rate is due. Working on a public holiday ordinarily earns holiday gross pay plus an additional day at the basic rate; overtime applies beyond normal hours. By mutual agreement, the day may be substituted. Part IV coverage limits which employees may use time off in lieu. Distinguish a holiday on a working day, non-working day, or rest day. For holiday gross pay, the employee must not be absent without consent or reasonable excuse on the working day immediately before or after the holiday; authorised leave on either day is permitted. No holiday pay is due when the holiday itself falls during approved unpaid leave. Additional basic-rate pay is the default for working on the holiday; substitute-holiday arrangements require mutual agreement. An employee outside Employment Act coverage is governed by the contract. Time off in lieu of hours worked is available only to employees not covered by Part IV under the stated arrangement. Rest-day pay and any excess-hours overtime are separate entitlements. A case-specific conclusion requires: Employment Act and Part IV coverage. Work schedule and whether the date is a working, non-working or rest day. Whether the employee worked, hours worked, agreed substitution/time-off arrangements, and relevant absence or unpaid-leave facts. Does not decide a specific date’s gazetted holiday status or compute holiday pay without schedule and wage facts. Does not replace separate rest-day, overtime or part-time rules. #### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA XBRL financial statement filing requirements and exemptions** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA says all Singapore-incorporated companies must prepare financial statements, except dormant relevant companies, and must file them unless exempted. A solvent exempt private company may qualify not to file; dormant-relevant-company relief requires all Companies Act section 201A conditions. Newly incorporated or inactive status alone is not listed as an exemption in this guidance. For required filings, ACRA lists simplified XBRL plus an authorised PDF for smaller and non-publicly accountable companies; XBRL FSH (Banks) or XBRL FSH (Insurance) plus an authorised PDF for the regulated bank, finance and insurance group; PDF only for companies limited by guarantee or companies approved to use other standards; and Full XBRL without a separate PDF copy for all other Singapore-incorporated companies required to file financial statements. “Smaller” requires both current-year revenue and assets not exceeding S$500,000. “Non-publicly accountable” also excludes listed and specified regulated entity types. ACRA labels technical resources as applying from 19 October 2026 onwards and identifies ACRA Taxonomy 2026 resources. A company must first determine whether it is required to file financial statements; dormant relevant companies and solvent EPCs may qualify for separate financial-statement exceptions. Small-company revenue and asset thresholds must both be met; group consolidation and currency translation details apply under the ACRA definitions page. A solvent EPC meeting an EPC definition may elect not to file financial statements but may file voluntarily; its annual-return solvency declaration still applies. Foreign companies with Singapore branches and some individually approved cases are addressed elsewhere on the ACRA filing guidance and are not classified by this local-company rule summary. ### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Withholding tax filing and payment deadline** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS requires WHT filing and payment by the 15th of the second month after its defined date of payment. For most payments, use the earliest of the contractual due date (or invoice date if there is no agreement, ignoring credit terms), credit to an account designated by the non-resident, and actual payment. Director fees have separate timing rules based on arrears/advance approval, entitlement, credit and actual payment. WHT still must be filed when a DTA or ARI makes the rate zero. GIRO is normally deducted on the 25th of the due month, or the next working day if that date is a weekend/public holiday. The exact deadline requires the payment type and all relevant dates. [IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/withholding-tax/withholding-tax-filing/withholding-tax-filing-and-payment-due-date)

**Source:** IRAS | Withholding Tax (WHT) filing and payment due date (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): WHT must be filed even if the payment to a non-resident is exempted under the Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreement (DTA) or Approved Royalties Incentive (ARI).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): As a payer, you must file and pay WHT to IRAS by the 15th of the second month from the date of payment to the non-resident.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): The date of payment is defined as the earliest of the following dates: For all payments except director's fees • When the payment is due and payable based on the agreement or contract, or the date of the invoice in the absence of any agreement or contract (credit terms should not be taken into consideration). • When payment is credited to the account of the non-resident or any other account(s) designated by the non-resident • The date of actual payment
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): For director's fees • When the payment is due and payable under the following scenarios: ◦ Director's fees approved in arrears For director's fees approved in arrears, the director has already rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned. However, the director's fees must be disclosed to and approved by members of the company before they can be paid to him. Hence, the earliest date on which the director is entitled to the director's fees, is the date the fees are voted and approved at the company's AGM. ◦ Director's fees approved in advance For director's fees approved in advance, the director may not have rendered the requisite services for the accounting year concerned when the fees are approved at the company's AGM. Hence, the earliest date on which the director can be entitled to the director's fees, is as and when he renders his services.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): If you are on GIRO for WHT payment, the GIRO deduction date is on the 25th of the month the tax is due. If the GIRO deduction date falls on a weekend or public holiday, the deduction will be made on the next working day.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Withholding tax filing and payment deadline): If you have made multiple payments to the same non-resident professional or non-resident public entertainer for the same engagement within a 60-day period, you can consolidate the various payments into 1 filing and declare the last payment date as the date of payment to the non-resident professional or public entertainer.

The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion

Updates on 21 May 2026
To further strengthen the retirement adequacy of senior employees, there will be an increase to the CPF contribution rates from 1 Jan 2027. Find out more about these changes and how it affects you and your employees.
Current rates
What are the CPF contribution rates?
The following table summarises the current contribution rates for Singaporeans and SPRs (from third year and onwards) with monthly wages above $750, across the different age groups.
Employee’s age (years) | Contribution rates from 1 January 2026 (monthly wages > $750)
By employer (% of wage) | By employee (% of wage) | Total (% of wage)
55 and below | 17 | 20 | 37
Above 55 to 60 | 16 | 18 | 34
Above 60 to 65 | 12.5 | 12.5 | 25
Above 65 to 70 | 9 | 7.5 | 16.5
Above 70 | 7.5 | 5 | 12.5
View all tables (PDF, 0.2MB) for the full set of contribution rate tables covering all citizenship statuses and SPR years.
Computation
Determine your employees’ CPF contributions
CPF contribution rates vary based on your employee’s citizenship status, age group, and total wages. As an employer, you are required to pay CPF contributions for your employees who are Singapore Citizens or Singapore Permanent Residents and who are earning total wages of more than $50 per month.
Step 1: Select the contribution rate table based on citizenship status
Select the contribution rate table that applies to your employee.
Table 1: Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR) from the third year of SPR status
Table 2: SPR in the first year of SPR status
Table 3: SPR in the second year of SPR status
Please ensure that your employees inform you the date when they became Singapore Citizens or SPRs, as different CPF contribution rates are applicable.
Determine the year of SPR status
The first year begins on the day of SPR conversion
The second year begins on the first day of the month after the first anniversary of SPR conversion
The third year begins on the first day of the month after the second anniversary of SPR conversion
Contribute more for first and second year SPRs
You and your employee who is in the first two years of SPR status can jointly apply to contribute CPF at a higher rate. The options are:
You and your employee both contribute at full rates (Table 1)
You contribute at full rates while your employee continues to contribute at graduated rates (Tables 4 and 5)
Step 2: Determine the rates based on age group and wage band
Different rates apply to different age groups.
New contribution rates apply from the first day of the month after the employee’s 55th, 60th, 65th or 70th birthday.
Different rates apply for different wage bands.
Step 3: Determine the Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
Apply the wage ceilings to determine Total Wages subject to CPF contributions
An employee’s CPF contributions are computed based on the Total Wages payable in a calendar month.
Total Wages are made up of an employee’s Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages. Different ceilings apply to Ordinary Wages and Additional Wages.
Step 4: Compute the CPF contributions on Total Wages
Compute Total CPF contributions
You can compute the total CPF contributions by applying the contribution rate to your employee’s total wages subject to CPF. The total CPF contributions comprise both your share as the employer and your employee’s share, which you are required to pay to the CPF Board. You are entitled to recover the employee’s share when paying your employee’s wages for the month.
Note that if your employee earns above $50 but not more than $500 per month, there is no employee’s share of CPF contributions. You will still need to pay the employer’s share.
Round off your Total CPF contributions
Please round off the Total CPF contributions to the nearest dollar. Cents should be dropped for amounts less than 50 cents, and amounts of 50 cents and above should be treated as an additional dollar. The cents should always be dropped for the employee’s share of CPF contributions.

As a Singapore Permanent Resident (SPR), you are required to make CPF contributions on wages earned in Singapore.
CPF contributions are not payable for employees who are neither Singapore Citizens nor SPRs.
Your CPF contribution rates as an SPR depend on how long you have held Permanent Resident status.
First-year rate: Applies from the day you obtain your SPR status, [i.e. the date indicated on your Entry Permit (Form 5/5A) issued by the Immigration & Checkpoints Authority (ICA)] until the last day of the month of your first anniversary of SPR.
Second-year rate: Applies from the month following your first anniversary as an SPR until the last day of the month of your second anniversary.
Third-year rate: Applies from the month following your second anniversary as an SPR onwards.
Example
If you have obtained your SPR status on 15 January 2026, the start and end dates for first, second and third year of obtaining SPR status are shown in the table below:
Year of obtaining SPR status | Starts from | Ends on
First year | 15 January 2026 | 31 January 2027
Second year | 1 February 2027 | 31 January 2028
Third year | 1 February 2028 | Not applicable

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**Final salary payment deadlines by termination reason** (party in scope: Employee)
- **MOM rule explanation:** For employees covered by the Employment Act, final salary is due on the last employment day when required notice is served; within 7 days of the last employment day when the employee resigns without notice; and, after misconduct dismissal or employer termination, on the last day or, if that is not possible, within 3 working days from dismissal or termination. Commission timing follows the employment contract or existing policies or practices. For a foreign employee leaving employment, the employer must withhold monies due for tax clearance for up to 30 days after notifying the Comptroller of Income Tax; this can affect when salary is released. - **Verified official source excerpt** (supports Final salary payment deadlines by termination reason): If you are covered by the Employment Act, your employer must pay your salary at least once a month.
They can also pay it at shorter intervals if they choose.
Salary must be paid:
Within 7 days after the end of the salary period.
For overtime work, within 14 days after the end of the salary period.

Your final salary payment could vary depending on the following situations:
In this situation | Your final salary must be paid
Employee resigns and serves the required notice period | On the last day of employment.
Employee resigns and does not serve the notice period | Within 7 days of the last day of employment.
Dismissal on grounds of misconduct | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of dismissal.
Employer terminates the contract | On the last day of employment. If this is not possible, then within 3 working days from date of termination.

If your contract involves commission, how and when the commission is paid depends on what is in your employment contract or existing policies or practices.
If you’re a foreign employee who is leaving your employment, your employer is required to withhold all your monies due to you for tax clearance for up to 30 days upon giving notice of the cessation of your employment to the Comptroller of Income Tax. The monies include your salary, leave pay, etc.

### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**IRAS company income-tax record retention and responsible person** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** A company must retain source documents, accounting records and schedules, bank statements and other transaction-connected business records for at least five years from the relevant Year of Assessment (YA). IRAS gives examples: records for YA 2019 are retained to 31 December 2023, while records for YA 2023 are retained to 31 December 2027. For a company struck off and dissolved, the officer immediately before dissolution keeps the books and papers for at least five years after dissolution; for a wound-up company, the liquidator does so for at least five years from dissolution. Use the relevant YA for ordinary company tax records; the page’s examples distinguish December and non-December financial-year ends. After dissolution, the source identifies a different responsible person and starts the five-year period from dissolution. This is corporate income tax record guidance, not the separate GST record-retention rule. The ordinary YA period does not replace the separate dissolution-date duties for struck-off or wound-up companies. For case-specific application, consider: The relevant YA and financial-year period. Whether the company was struck off and dissolved or wound up, and its dissolution date. The source examples explain ordinary YA retention; they do not determine every record-specific retention requirement. A company-specific last-retention date requires the correct YA or dissolution date. For YA 2025, retain the records through at least 31 December 2029. The proposed disposal date 01/10/2029 is before the end of that period, so do not shred the records then. Filing the tax return does not end the retention period. #### CPF Board — CPF contributions

**Status:** Evidence verified

**CPF employer refund timing and application requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **CPF rule explanation:** Refund requests for CPF contributions generally must be made immediately and no later than one year from payment; the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” field identifies the payment date. For conditional wages, the one-year period instead runs from when the wages are due to be repaid to the employer, as stated in employment terms or a mutual agreement, and that date must be entered in the application. Before applying, the employer must return the employee share directly to the employee. CPF Board effects refunds only to the extent of funds available in the employee’s CPF account. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions should be claimed promptly; excess CPF Annual Limit contributions paid from 2023 are automatically refunded to the employer’s Direct Debit Account from February 2024. The general and entire-submission application deadline is one year from contribution payment, using the “PAYMENTS RECEIVED ON” record field. Conditional-wage refunds use the repayment due date, not the contribution payment date. The employer must first return the employee share where applicable; refunds depend on funds available in employee CPF accounts. Excess Additional Wage ceiling contributions are a prompt-application category. CPF Annual Limit excess contributions paid from 2023 are refunded automatically to the employer from February 2024; this is distinct from an application for an AW-ceiling refund. For case-specific application, consider: Refund category and CPF payment date. For conditional wages, the contractual or mutually agreed repayment due date. Whether the employee share was returned and funds remain available in CPF account(s). For AW or annual-limit excess, the relevant year and excess category. Do not infer a refund deadline when the payment date, conditional-wage repayment date or calendar anniversary is unclear. The source does not establish that a particular refund application will be accepted or the amount CPF Board will refund. ### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

#### Ministry of Manpower — Employment requirements

**Status:** Evidence verified

**MOM itemised payslip issue and delivery requirements** (party in scope: Employer)
- **MOM rule explanation:** Employers must issue itemised pay slips to employees covered by the Employment Act together with payment. If that is not possible, the pay slip must be given within three working days of payment. For termination or dismissal, it must be given together with outstanding salary. MOM allows a soft or hard copy, including handwritten. The pay slip must include the employer and employee names, payment date, basic salary, salary period, applicable allowances, other payments, deductions and total net salary; overtime hours, pay and period are included where applicable. If payments are made more than once a month, pay slips may be consolidated, but the consolidated slip must show all payments since the last slip. Employers must retain issued pay slips: the latest two years for current employees, and the last two years for ex-employees for one year after they leave. The requirements apply to employees covered by the Employment Act. Only applicable pay slip items need to be shown; overtime items 9 to 11 need not be included when overtime pay does not apply. The fallback is three working days after payment only when the employer cannot give the pay slip with payment. Consolidation is permitted for multiple monthly payments, but must include every payment since the previous slip. Items that do not apply need not be shown; MOM’s page gives overtime items as an example. This rule does not calculate final-salary deadlines or determine Employment Act coverage for a particular worker. For case-specific application, consider: Employment Act coverage. ### Statutory Compliance & Legal Authority

**Whole-question status:** Verified general guidance is available. Evidence verified for mapped issues; full request coverage unconfirmed.

**Individual applicability:** General guidance does not by itself establish eligibility or compliance in an individual case.
**Material evidence gaps:** None identified within the listed guidance. Full request coverage still requires an independent assessment.

#### ACRA — Corporate filing and governance

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ACRA company secretary appointment and sole-director requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **ACRA rule explanation:** ACRA’s guide says every company must have a company secretary, appointed within six months of successful registration, and the position cannot remain vacant for more than six months. The director may face a fine of up to S$1,000 if the vacancy exceeds that period. The guide says the secretary must be a real person who is a Singapore citizen, permanent resident, or otherwise meets the local residency rules; the sole director cannot also be the company secretary. The secretary’s administrative role includes maintaining company information and registers, organising and recording meetings, reminding directors of annual filing deadlines, and updating them on new rules. This overview is not a complete statutory eligibility check: verify the Companies Act requirements for residence, non-debarment and knowledge or experience, plus any additional public-company qualifications, before concluding that a candidate qualifies. See section 171: https://sso.agc.gov.sg/Act/CoA1967?ProvIds=pr171- [Step 4.3: Choosing company directors & other key officers | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority](https://www.acra.gov.sg/register/business/registering-different-business-structures/local-company/appointing-company-directors-other-key-officers/)

**Source:** Step 4.3: Choosing company directors & other key officers | Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ACRA company secretary appointment and sole-director requirements): Every company must have at least one company director and one company secretary.

A secretary must be appointed within six months of successful registration. The position cannot be empty for more than six months. Otherwise, the director may face a fine of up to $1,000.

Directors run the company and decide on its strategy and direction.

Under the Companies Act, company directors must:

•

• Be ordinarily resident

•

•

• Be 18 years old or older

•

•

• Be mentally fit to make decisions

•

•

• Be a Singapore citizen, Singapore permanent resident, or someone who meets local residency rules

•

•

• Not be banned from being a director

•

•

• Not be disqualified from acting as a director of a company (for example, an undischarged bankrupt)

•

Note: If you are a Foreign Identification Number (FIN) holder, check with your pass issuer (such as Ministry of Manpower (MOM) (opens in new tab) or Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA) (opens in new tab)) before you accept a role.

All company directors have a key duty to follow the Companies Act.

Duties and penalties

What you need to know

Details

•

• Keep proper records

•

•

• Prepare financial reports (when needed)

•

•

• File required documents with ACRA on time

•

•

• Act in the company's best interests

•

Note: You cannot be an “inactive director”, “nominee director”, or “sleeping director”. All directors are responsible under the legislation, whether active or not.

Penalties

Directors who do not meet these duties may face penalties. Depending on severity, these may include:

•

• Fines up to $5,000

•

•

• Up to two years in jail

•

•

• Being banned from being a director for five years

•

New directors can take a free Directors Training Programme. The two-hour course covers:

•

• Director requirements

•

•

• Your key duties and responsibilities under the Companies Act

•

•

• Tax filing information

•

•

• Employee Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions

•

•

• Workplace safety rules

•

Tip: This programme also includes important information from other government agencies.

Nominee directors act as directors for your company, but represent another person or entity. This happens when the director is required (formally or informally) to follow the directions, instructions, or wishes of another person. The person or entity they represent is called the nominator.

On the date of your company's incorporation, the nominee director needs to:

•

• Inform the company that they are a nominee director.

•

•

• Provide the nominator's details.

•

Company secretaries help the company to comply with its requirements.

A company secretary must:

•

• Be a real person (not a company)

•

•

• Be a Singapore citizen, Singapore permanent resident, or someone who meets local residency rules

•

•

• Not be the same person as the sole director

•

Company secretaries handle administrative work, including:

•

• Maintaining their local company's information and registers or maintaining their foreign company's information

•

•

• Organising meetings and taking notes

•

•

• Reminding directors about annual filing deadlines

•

•

• Updating everyone on any new rules

The position cannot be empty for more than six months. Otherwise, the director may face a fine of up to $1,000.

#### IRAS — Corporate income tax

**Status:** Evidence verified

**ECI filing and waiver requirements** (party in scope: Company)
- **IRAS rule explanation:** IRAS generally requires ECI filing within three months after FYE. The general waiver requires both annual revenue of S$5 million or less for that financial year and nil ECI for the YA, with ECI measured before partial or start-up exemption. Revenue is the company’s main source of income; for an investment holding company it is investment income. A nil ECI or book loss alone does not qualify a company whose relevant revenue exceeds S$5 million; likewise, revenue below the threshold does not qualify when ECI is positive. IRAS gives separate entity categories that need not file and says companies self-assess the waiver. To assess a particular YA, confirm FYE, principal/investment revenue, pre-exemption ECI and any specifically excluded category. [IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing](https://www.iras.gov.sg/taxes/corporate-income-tax/estimated-chargeable-income-(eci)-filing)

**Source:** IRAS | Estimated Chargeable Income (ECI) Filing (live external)
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): ECI is an estimate of your company's taxable profits (after deducting tax-allowable expenses) for a Year of Assessment (YA).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company has to file ECI within 3 months from the end of your financial year unless: • Your company qualifies for the ECI filing waiver; or • Your company is specifically not required to file ECI.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company does not need to file ECI in any Year of Assessment (YA) when both criteria are met: • Annual revenue1 is $5 million or below for the financial year; and • ECI is nil for the YA. The ECI should be the amount before deducting the exempt amount under the partial tax exemption scheme or the tax exemption scheme for new start-up companies.
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Revenue refers to a company's main source of income and excludes separate source income, such as interest, dividend and rental, which does not arise from its principal activity. In the case of an investment holding company, the revenue is its investment income (e.g. dividend income and interest income).
- **Verified official source excerpt** (supports ECI filing and waiver requirements): Your company is required to self-assess if it qualifies for the ECI filing waiver.
